utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. A.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to continue from where we left off yesterday, and I should like to ask the usher to show you document P54.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you put it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. A, on this map, could you please take a look at number 3. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is that where your house is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need the document any more. Mr. A, you told us yesterday that -- I apologise, but could I ask the technical booth to lower the ELMO so I can see the witness better when I am addressing him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this helps, doesn't it? You can see me better. Am I a handsome guy?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, gold all over. On the corner of your house, you saw two photographers standing at the corner to your house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, from the corner of Uska Street and Stradun to the city bell tower, how far is that distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's about 80 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Petrovic. Microphone for counsel. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 13, line 2 of the transcript, you said yesterday that you yourself, from the distance that you were at, were not able to recognise the victim that was lying below the bell tower; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 13, line 25 this time, in response to a question from my colleague Mr. Re as to whether you were able to recognise the clothing that the victim was wearing, you said yes -- you said no, you couldn't even recognise the colours from that distance. So you concluded that it was victim Pavo Urban exclusively on the basis of what the photo reporters told you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I heard their story, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your conclusion, therefore, was made on the basis of what you heard them talking about; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 13, line 7, my learned friend Mr. Re asked you whether you had seen what the victim was wearing, and on page 13, line 14, your answer was that he was wearing some sort of vest. It says "very dark coloured" in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He always wore that kind of vest as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 13 once again, line 7, my colleague explicitly asked you the following: "What was he wearing that particular day? What did the victim have on him that particular day?" And your answer to that question by my colleague was this: "A very, very dark coloured vest." Further on, when you took a look at the photograph provided by Mr. Re, you immediately changed your opinion and said, "Yes, yes. It was a red vest." Now, why, sir -- why, Mr. A, did you first say -- when directly asked what the person was wearing that day, your answer was, "A very, very dark coloured vest."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You didn't link up the facts properly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me where I went wrong then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he usually wore a red vest -- black vest --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's correction: Black vest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when we were together. And on this photograph I can see -- I saw that it was a red vest, which meant that it wasn't the vest he usually wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, are there any problems with the interpretation in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is my impression that your words were not properly interpreted again, although I gave you the page and line where it says what you said before this Trial Chamber yesterday. So I'm asking you, is everything all right in the interpretation, not to go on with any mistakes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, everything is all right. Yesterday on the photograph I saw a red vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Everything you told us yesterday about the position of the victim, what was next to the victim, is in fact what you deduced by looking at the photograph shown to you by my colleague yesterday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Everything else or, rather, the other thing that I want to ask you today about where the man was lying, the position he was in, et cetera, that would have no sense because you are only deducing it on the basis of the picture my colleague handed to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true. I saw the body myself underneath the bell tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to tell us whether during the shelling you ever went into the second part of your house, where Mrs. Aleksic was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that day, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, why did you then tell us yesterday, Mr. A, when we were looking at the video excerpt, why did you indicate Mrs. Aleksic's windows as being the windows through which you allegedly saw the body of the victim lying underneath the bell tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. A, the statement you gave to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A lot of time has gone by since then. I know the general gist of the statement and the chronology, which I consider to be the most important thing. Now the details that you are highlighting are obviously ones that you yourself require.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that yesterday you said on page 14, line 19, that your colleagues -- or the colleagues of the victim had risked their lives had they tried to pull the body away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also told us that you took a look through the window, told your wife -- and went to tell your wife that the victim, that the person had been hit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that the victim was lying down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I assume your wife was in the bathroom all the time. How much time did it take you to go back to the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About half a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 15, line 5 of the transcript, you said the following: "Underneath the window I saw an ambulance, and the ambulance had reached the person." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came up to the window, the ambulance was on its way to the bell tower, the direction being west-east, and I saw the ambulance reach the body and then I no longer saw the body. At that point in time, I went back to tell them in the bathroom that the ambulance had indeed arrived, and when I went back to the window, they managed to put the body into the ambulance very quickly, and I no longer saw the ambulance either. That's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you first saw the ambulance coming up to the victim underneath the bell tower, and then you saw the ambulance leaving; is that right? Or did you go into the bathroom to tell your wife that the ambulance had arrived? What was the sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got to the window, I saw a car coming. I -- I had the need to go back to the window to see what was happening, and I saw the vehicle go past my window, underneath my window, and I could clearly see that it was a white van with red stripes down the middle with the Red Cross sign on it, the Red Cross emblem, and I watched this throughout. I saw the ambulance drive towards the victim up until the point when the ambulance was between me and the victim and I was no longer able to see the victim lying down, just the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that time, the material time that we're talking about, the shelling of that particular area was not going on. There was no shelling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The shelling was most intense at that point in time, and shells were falling all around quite close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: During that interval, you said yesterday that they were falling every second. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it correct? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the feeling I had. Yes, it is right. It was all hell breaking loose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you went outside again, you couldn't see the victim or the ambulance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were any other vehicles passing by the Stradun at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No other cars, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you have heard any other car if it passed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would, because the window is about four metres up from the Stradun, maximum of four metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other people on the Stradun at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody except the two photographers at the corner of Stradun and Uska Street. So just up by my building on the western facade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, how long was the victim lying down under the bell tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I heard the screams saying, "Pavo's been hit, Pavo's been hit," by the two photographers, that's when I went up to the window and I clearly saw below the bell tower the body. It was motionless, lying on the ground, and I went back and said what I'd seen. So as far as I could see, all this lasted perhaps five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anybody standing around the body of the victim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody try to assist the victim underneath the bell tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, I was preparing to go outside, and had the two photographers rushed out into the open space, they would certainly have been killed with all the shells that were falling round about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At that -- the moment that the body was lying underneath the bell tower, were shells falling on the Stradun itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The shells were falling in that part, on the western side of the Stradun, too. In all parts of that area around St. Blaise Church and thereabouts. And I really don't know how nobody else was killed, the people from the ambulance, for example. It's really amazing. I always wondered how they managed to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we now play a video clip, but we're not on such good terms by far with the technical booth as my colleague on the opposite side, so there may be some problems there, but I hope we will do all right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You weren't in town then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid -- yes, the technical booth -- it seems to be all right now. We can see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Stop. Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. A, can you see this? Is this the bell tower area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's below the bell tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And is this the body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's where the body was, but the position of the body was different when I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, would you please explain to us how the body changed its posture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably under the pain that the person was suffering.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this -- stop. Stop the tape there, please. Thank you. Is this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: May we have a fast forward, please, and then stop. Stop there. Is there the space around St. Blaise Church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Orlando's monument has been protected by wooden planks there that you can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle is this? What kind of car is this, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't seen this car.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can shells be seen on this footage, those that are falling in this area of Stradun towards the Pile Gate and also the St. Blaise Church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can shells be seen on a still photograph?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, was this vehicle passing by at the moment when the victim was lying underneath the town bell tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From the moment when the victim was hit up to the moment when the ambulance arrived, if five minutes went by and if you were following all the time what was going on, how come you didn't see this, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was at a different time. I just described the time when I heard the voices of his colleagues, and I described those five minutes when this was happening. Now, when the late person got killed is something I don't know. I myself do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So perhaps he was hit half an hour, an hour, or two hours earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. A, you basically don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, do you know that this victim died of bleeding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I found out about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this victim died because he lay there for hours and nobody gave him any kind of assistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because nobody could have helped the victim. The situation was not a normal one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, does that differ from what you said to us here yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I said anything different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, now we are going to deal with the statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in the month of September 2002. So we're talking about page -- let me actually try to find the English version for my learned friends. The last paragraph on page 4 of the English version. This is what you say, Mr. A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "During the day I saw from the window of my apartment when a friend of mine was hit by a shell, Pavo Urban. He was a journalist and photographer."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please wait for me to put the question to you. Sir, why did you say that you saw from the window when your friend was hit? Why did you not tell the investigators the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to that. I object to it on two bases. First of all, the suggestion that the witness is lying; and secondly, if you read the sentence, it is actually ambiguous. Is says: "Sometime during the day I saw from the window of apartment, my friend Pavo Urban, a journalist and photographer --" Sorry: "... Pavo Urban, a journalist and photographer, hit by a shell." The way it's translated into English, "hit" can be read two ways. The way it's put, "hit" could be, "I saw him, he had been hit by a shell," or, "I saw him being hit by a shell." It's the way it's written. The mere fact that it's translated this way doesn't mean the witness said it in that way nor that he's not telling the truth now. So I object on those two bases. I mean, of course we know, because he gives his statement in Croatian, it's then translated in English, read back to him in Croatian, my learned friend now reads it to the translators in Croatian -- in Croatian and it comes back in English again. So it gets translated three or four or five times, so you lose all the nuances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue pursuing the matter, Mr. Petrovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, when do you tell the truth, Mr. A? Do you tell the truth at all? Did you tell the truth to the investigators or did you tell the truth yesterday to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I came here guided by my own conscience in order to lessen the suffering of all in the former Yugoslavia and to finally get rid of the anathema over the entire area so that all ethnic groups, the Serb and Montenegrin people, inter alia, should live a normal life and we should not slaughter each other every half a century. That was my objective. That's why I came here. I came here for the general good. I did not come here to lie or because I wish your client any evil. Those who should try him can try him. I'm not trying anybody. I came here to tell the truth. Your Honours, I had to say this because this is my motive, why I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, you would help the Honourable Trial Chamber the most if you would tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm only telling the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence, Mr. A: "He was hit at a distance of about 20 metres from my apartment." Obviously you are talking about this as if it were something that you were watching yourself. Why did you tell the investigator that? Did he not understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's probably the way I put it, about 20 metres away, but at that moment I wasn't really thinking about it. At the time I had that feeling. I mean, I never actually did any measuring. Later on, when I walked around Stradun, I know how long my steps are, I sort of realised how long it was, but it's not that much of a difference, and this seems so important to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence, Mr. A: "He fell down and was lying on his stomach."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: "He fell down on his stomach." When was it that you saw him falling and when was it that you saw him lying on his stomach?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that several times yesterday. You are trying to set me on a collision course. You are trying to say that I'm contradicting myself. I saw him lying immobile, and it is in that context that I interpreted this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, did somebody misinterpret what you were saying again? Yesterday you said that he was lying on his back, and today you said that he was lying on his stomach. Is it a mistake in the interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the photograph that was shown to me, he was lying on his back, and that's the same photograph you showed just now. That's the picture that was shown to me yesterday, too, except that it was a close-up. I myself saw him in a spasm, lying on his left hip. His feet were facing the north, his head was facing the south. So that's the way it was. If you have any feeling of space, that was it. I saw him lying that way, in that position.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, because of the special measures involved this time, I have to keep my microphone off and then I have to put -- turn it on again, but I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before we go on, can I ask my learned friend to say where in the transcript he said yesterday he was lying on his back. I've just done a search of the transcript and I can see at line 13:10 he said: "He was lying on his left hip, as if he were crouching, facing the west."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was it the evidence or the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In reference to the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My learned friend just said, "Yesterday you said he was lying --" "Yesterday you said --" line 25 -- sorry, page 25, line 3. "Yesterday you said he was lying on his back and today you said he was lying on his stomach. Is this a mistake in the interpretation?" I assume my learned friend is referring to "Yesterday you said in the transcript..." I can't find it. If it's there, I just ask him to point it out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday Mr. Re showed a photograph, and everything this witness said about the position of the body was on page 13. Everything he said, he said on the basis of that photograph. Not in a single word did he refer to anything else but what he saw in the photograph. Your Honour, on this photograph, as he confirmed today, the man is lying on his back. So everything else is misinterpretation. Not in a single word did he mention what he said today, that he was lying on his stomach. These are two completely different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's just incorrect. The only question I asked was at 13:1 -- 13:3, "What position was the body lying?" Answer: "He was lying on his left hip --" which I understand to be at the front of the body -- "as if he were crouching, facing the west." I then showed him the photograph and asked him what he -- how he identified it, and he identified the photograph of the person Pavo Urban, not of the person lying as he saw him. That wasn't the purpose of showing him the photograph; it was the identity of Mr. Urban who he'd said his face he couldn't recognise from so far away. To put to the witness that he said one thing yesterday and another now is just incorrect. He did not say yesterday in evidence that he saw Mr. Urban lying on his back or at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, did you say to us yesterday here that you saw Pavo Urban lying on his stomach? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that I ever said that he was lying any other way but on his stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So yesterday you said to us here that he was lying on his stomach.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I described him, as I described him as he was lying there. I could not have seen anything else. Anything else would be a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. A, where he was hit, where Pavo Urban was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean which part of his body? I mean, don't make me read your mind, read your thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the victim you saw lying below the city bell tower was hit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard later from what people were saying that he was hit in the stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now your statement of three years ago goes on to say: "I think he died several moments after he was hit." Mr. A, how did you know that? Why didn't you say exactly what you knew about this or, rather, that you didn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All those statements were based on stories and what I learnt from others, in this specific case from his colleagues. And I asked them afterwards, and they said that he expired within the space -- that he was motionless within the space of ten seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. A. You should have told us that much earlier on, and that would have shortened the time that we have spent here in front of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was you who did not conduct the process properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you now, Mr. A, I put it to you that you didn't see any of this, that since 5.00 in the morning until 8.00 in the evening, longer than anybody else in the Old Town, you sat in your bathroom and that all this is what you construed on the basis of the stories told by others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, and this is on page 19, line 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this new subject matter, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we might have a break now, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, would you please describe for us the damage done to the house you lived in between Izmedju Polaca number 10. And you said that this occurred on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The greatest damage was to the roof construction as well as to the facade, the result of shrapnels and explosive devices which caused cracks, et cetera. On my part of the roof the western belvedere window was completely damaged and just held on by a piece of tin. But on the western side there was a large hole and a smaller hole, as I've already said, which was superimposed or, rather, right above the big hole. On the eastern side of Mrs. Aleksic's part of the roof --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about your house. Is that all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me first, please, on the belvedere, the one that was seriously damaged, the hole, as you said a moment ago if I understood you correctly, was facing west.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The belvedere was hit face on. It was just the hole that was more towards the west, on the flat area of the roof or, rather, the slant of the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That was the only damage on your half of the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But from the explosion, the domes were shifted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you tell us yesterday that the partition walls had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read that from a report written by an expert. And yes, they were. The partition walls were damaged. Parts of the facade were in ruins and rubbles, and all the debris from the roof fell inside, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the real damage you described in response to my question. All the rest you read from the report that was before you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert myself. I'm not a civil engineer, so that's what I did. I myself am a technologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But I'm sure you can remember the damage done to your own house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the roof was destroyed --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: All right. You've told us that. Thank you, that will do. You also told us yesterday that the hit to the belvedere was a hit by a mortar. It was a mortar projectile of 120 millimetres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that there were two hits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And I deduced that from the holes, the two holes, the larger hole and the smaller hole, which were partially superimposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you therefore consider that the two mortar mines hit the same place, shells hit the same place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, roughly the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you can see the two different hits; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I judge that by the diameter of the circle, the aperture that was caused.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to the people from the institute who came to assess the damage in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I wasn't at home that day, so they took the stabiliser fin from the couch that I described, otherwise I would have kept it as a trophy to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who gave them this information, what was hit, how much damage was done? Your wife, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My wife let them into the apartment, and they did an on-site investigation and drew up a report. That's the way they work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So they toured the apartment on their own and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did your wife tell you how much time they spent in the apartment? Because it's a large house, a tall house, five levels.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She did say that they were there for about 15 or 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who told them that your house had been hit by an 82-millimetre projectile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. You should ask them that. I don't know whether they are professional enough to be able to determine for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So this fin from the shell that you found, you established that it was a 120-millimetre one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You knew that at that point in time, as you did your military service, were interested in artillery pieces, and that the calibre was written down on the fin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the cap. And that's what it said. And I found this mark. When I was mobilised later on, I had occasion to hold a shell and the capsule and the fin of that kind in my hand, so I knew that was it. And I know what an 80-millimetre shell is and a 120-millimetre one. I can compare it to the parts of my body in size.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If your part of the house was hit twice, do you know why the institute recorded only one hit on your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably of the lack of professional training. They're not forensic experts. They're not professionals in matters of projectiles, I assume. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So in addition to that, they didn't gather up information from people who could tell them something; you, or your future wife, or anybody like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't actually ask them. I had no personal contact with them at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And a moment ago you told us that they took that stabiliser fin away with them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I now ask the usher, please, to show the witness Exhibit P98.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, can you see on the transcript that you read yesterday that it says that it was an 82 projectile that had allegedly hit your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So that's probably a mistake, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the description of the damage done, we can see just one direct hit. So I assume they were wrong there, too, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: They also mention in their report something that you failed to mention yourself, some partition walls and so on. I assume they were wrong there, too, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I assume they're more professional there than I am. I saw it visually, but I'm not able to assess the statics and the damage done to the statics of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, would you be so kind as to tell me, please -- or, rather, take a look at the photograph, and it's on page 3 of the document before you. Is it true that this photograph is a photograph of the house where Mrs. Aleksic lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That's right, because I can see the corner of one side of the house and not the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know something about the damage done on Mrs. Aleksic's part of the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as Mrs. Aleksic's roof is concerned, I went to take a look at that the next day and it seemed to be far greater. And I know that because the right-hand side -- so there are two owners, of the left-hand side and the right-hand side of the building. The right side is the owner of my part of the house, and in the 1970s, he renovated the entire roof construction. So it was far more resistant and in a better condition to suffer damage of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how large was the hole on Mrs. Aleksic's roof, on her half of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't actually see the hole because the whole roof was razed. It was eliminated. So all that was left was the wooden construction and the beams. And it was only looking at the beams that you were able to see where the projectile actually hit the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that there was no roof. No roof remained on Mrs. Aleksic's part of the house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, just the bearing beams. But otherwise, no tiles or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the previous document, which refers to Izmedju Polaca Street number 8, that house. How come the experts failed to record what you yourself personally saw?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How can he answer that? I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does it say in this document that is before you, Mr. A, what you have just told us? It says: "Direct blow against the roof destroyed a part of the roof construction, approximately 16 square metres." You said there were no tiles left on the roof at all, so who is wrong; you or them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. It's a matter of interpretation, one's personal view of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, you will allow, Mr. A, for the fact that you can see if the roof has -- if a house has a roof or does not have a roof. That's not up to interpretation. Sixteen square metres is a small part of the roof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had in mind the bearing capacity of the roof, not the tiles, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you explain that to us? What do you mean by bearing capacity and construction of the roof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are the lateral bearing beams and the basic wooden construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But they didn't record what you yourself saw, and that is that not a single tile remained on Mrs. Aleksic's roof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I remember that because for a long time afterwards, on the whole roof there was a sort of rubber tarpaulin or plastic protective film because they didn't have time to repair the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say -- if I say that the professionals got it wrong and you got it right? Would that be the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my impression. I can't say that they got it wrong. I don't know who got it wrong, but the damage was much greater or appeared to be much greater in quantity. In quality, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So are you right when you say that there wasn't a single tile left standing on the roof or the people who say that just an area of 16 square metres suffered damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just giving you my own impressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In describing the damage done to the Old Town, yesterday you said that unfortunately on the Stradun - and you told us that on page 19, line 21 - vehicles weren't able to pass that way and nor were the pedestrians because of all the rubble on the Stradun; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us, please, were there large pieces of rock or tile or stone, or what it looked like generally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were stones and tiles and bits of wood of different shapes and sizes along the buildings themselves. And this was a thick layer which thinned off towards the centre of the street, the centre of Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The efforts made by the citizens of the Old Town, I assume, were geared towards clearing up the debris slowly. So how long did this take, how many days? After how many days were you able to walk that way more or less normally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said yesterday, at about 7.00 the fire brigade turned up to put the fire out on buildings that were burning, and after that fire brigade teams turned up. They were the only ones who had the necessary tools to clear up the rubble, and they went on cleaning late into the night. It was dark, so I assumed they had to stop this cleaning when it got really dark and then resume the next morning, and they went on until about 11.00, as we were able to see on one of the pictures shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that somebody during the night cleaned everything up, picked up all the rubble, the stones, the beams; that all that was cleared up during the night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That wasn't possible. Not everything could have been cleared up during the night. As some of it was to ensure normal necessary communication via the Stradun, which is the main street in town, and then they continued this cleaning up operation the next day until about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why 11.00? How come you know it was 11.00 precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that because I walked around and looked the next day. It was very cold. Nobody liked to go out much, and nobody did unless they had some business to attend to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, were you able to see this looking out of your window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did they start cleaning and finish cleaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I got up -- well, I was exhausted, so I got up sometime around 8.00 or 9.00, thereabouts. But while I was still lying in bed, I heard the work going on and the tools being used, the sounds of the clearing up underneath my window.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was a dredger used to pick up the rubble and debris?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that wasn't possible. They did it with their hands and shovels and picks and anything they had to hand, any tools that were to hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The film that my colleague Mr. Re showed you yesterday, that footage, that was taken when everything was cleaned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it appeared to me to be. So I can't tell you the exact time when it was filmed but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the film was taken around 11.00. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you know who took the film, who filmed it all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the film taken that same day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How do you mean the same day; the 7th? The 7th, the 6th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who mentioned the 7th, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why did you meaning the 7th, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because Stradun looked that way on the 7th in the afternoon. That's when it was cleared up. It was cleared up that morning, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, the Stradun was completely clear, if that was on the 7th, then on the 7th, the 8th, the 9th, the 20th. Where do you get the idea that this footage was taken on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume. I don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What do you base your assumptions on, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what I base my assumptions on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to anybody, Mr. A, from -- since yesterday? Between yesterday and today, did you discuss this matter with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, with no one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But you recognise the cleaned up Stradun of the 7th, for instance, and not the 27th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was like that throughout those days, roughly the same state.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you say you know that that was on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to this. Out of fairness to the witness, my learned friend should put -- remind the witness of the question I asked him yesterday in relation to the video at page 19:16, when I showed it to him and said, "Does that video clip we've just shown depict the state of the Stradun in the Old Town in Dubrovnik on the 7th of December 1991?" To which the answer was, "At this point in time the street had been cleaned considerably. There was far more debris before," and so on. Out of fairness, Mr. Petrovic should put that to the witness if he's suggesting that he's spoken to people overnight which have implanted in his mind the idea that the video I showed him yesterday and said -- suggested to him was the 7th was in fact the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I answer Mr. Re? It is precisely for the sake of fairness and equality in this courtroom that I'm putting this question. It is quite clear, it can be seen from the context of that answer, that the gentleman implicitly denies, implicitly denies that the recording was made on the 7th because everything was cleaned, and today he comes here with a different story. That's what causes my concern, Mr. Re. And that is only fair if one reads what he said in response to your question regarding the film of the 7th. Implicitly he denies that this was taken on the 7th because he said that everything was cleared, and that's what I'm asking him about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I must say what you see by way of implication is not something that I see. As I consider the answer that has been, and the question that have now been read by Mr. Re, it seemed to me the witness was saying, yes, this is a film showing how it was on the 7th after it had been cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, with your permission, I would just like to play that part of the tape now. This is Exhibit P78.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this a cleaned Stradun, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What time is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. These fire hoses were there only on that day on the Stradun. That's the only thing I can say. It's only if I had filmed this myself could I say anything with a high degree of certainty. It would be unfair for me to say anything for sure in relation to material that was made by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, this is what Stradun looked like when it was cleared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And the cleaning of Stradun happened overnight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In part during the night, but for the most part it was done in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was there an alert on that day, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That day? I can't remember. I cannot remember. There were so many that it's hard for me to place them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This looks as if it had been cleaned in great detail, as if all the dust had all been cleaned and everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, no. Not all the dust could have been cleaned.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is this in front of St. Blaise's Church?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. In front of the entrance into the church, on the northern side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell me why somebody did not carry away these rocks. These are pretty big rocks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably because every little piece of rock in the Old City is valuable. So it was probably there for the sake of restoration or other processes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please stop now. If you can rewind it a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How come nobody cleaned this, Mr. A?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They should be asked, those who did the cleaning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You saw pieces of rock, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Again, nobody had collected them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably for the same reason like the stones in front of Sveti Vlaho, same place; for the sake of restoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. A, please be so kind as to tell us the following: During the night between the 6th and 7th of December, who decided which stones should be removed and which should not because they were important for restoration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know as much as you do about that. So that's my answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But somebody certainly did decide "We're going to clean this and we're not going to clear that."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Various institutions that were in charge of the Old Town and the heritage there, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Probably that night already they decided and made an assessment in terms of what should be cleared and what should not. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume you are. Perhaps it can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. A, do you considerably and unnecessarily, if I may say so, exaggerate in describing something that was truly a sad day in the history of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should like to assure everyone present in this courtroom today that I did not even tell half of the entire truth. I wished to be and I wish to be as objective as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is with regret that I have to say that I agree you did not say even half of the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to that last comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Could I indicate, before Mr. Re is heard, that it is a gratuitous comment that you made at the end. It was not a question, it was an observation on your assessment of the evidence. When put to a witness, that is not a proper way of conducting the hearing. You may, in your final submission to this Tribunal put submissions how we should evaluate the evidence of particular witnesses, but that's not your function at the present time. If you could bear that in mind for the future. Now, Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May I please, with your permission, say that this last part of the tape that we saw was a Prosecution exhibit, P78, and that Mr. A was shown from 18 minutes, 50 seconds, to the 22nd minute of that film. That footage was shown to Mr. A. And the first video clip that was used in the cross-examination was V000-1789. This was material that was disclosed to the Defence by the OTP, and the section from the 13th to the 15th minute of that material was used there. In view of the technical constraints that the Defence has, I await your instructions, Your Honour, in terms of whether I should try to have these clips copied and should I then tender them or is what I have done so far by way of marking it sufficient for the Trial Chamber at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to us to be adequate, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness A, you were asked a number of questions in cross-examination about your living in the village or area of Cilipi in September and October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown Exhibit P9, which is the Times map of the relevant portion of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness A, I just want you to locate the village of Cilipi in that area on the map and just point to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you just move it up a little bit. Can you move it up -- [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're indicating -- [B/C/S on English channel]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I seem to be getting B/C/S interpretation in my headphones. Are other people experiencing that? Is it okay now, the interpretation? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness A, you were pointing on the map somewhere near the Montenegrin border on the coast of Dubrovnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Re, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You described yesterday observing JNA patrols in the area. Was it within the territory of Croatia or did you go across the border into Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Radovcici is a Croat village within the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is the answer to my question no, you didn't go across the border into Montenegro and Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. Never at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May the exhibit be returned, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My learned friend Mr. Petrovic yesterday cross-examined you about the word "mobilisation" which appears in your statement and your correction of that to the Office of the Prosecutor and in court to "organised" or"self-organised." I want to show you the Croatian language version of the statement of the 14th and 18th of September, 2000. I've highlighted in yellow a portion on the fifth paragraph in which the word "mobilisation" has been used. Yesterday Mr. Petrovic referred to your use of the word "mobilisation," and this was the third example he used. I want you to read allowed to the Trial Chamber the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "As far as I know, our village had carried out mobilisation independently of others, not having received instructions from anyone. Actually, the situation was rather chaotic and there was not enough time to organise a real army and to develop a proper chain of command."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you read the next sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In addition to that, no one from the outside helped us. If the Territorial Defence from Dubrovnik did have some weapons, it had been stored in Trebinje."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have the statement back, please. And yesterday, although you said the word "mobilisation" had been or was more aptly described as "organised," is what you said, that portion that you just read out and is in your statement, is that a correct state of affairs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Except for the word "mobilisation."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You told the Trial Chamber yesterday that you were not given a copy of the statement, and the first time you saw or were given a written copy was when you came to The Hague in January this year. When did you realise the word "mobilisation" didn't quite accurately reflect what you describe as "organisation"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even then when this was translated to me orally after having completed my statement, I probably then indicated the mistakes in the translation as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Petrovic also questioned you about your relative Ivan Rados and what you -- what you had written in your statement, and he referred to a correction of the statement which he had which the Office of the Prosecutor provided to him after speaking to you. Again, when was the first time you realised, having had a chance to read the statement, that the statement wasn't entirely correct, and when did you offer the correction to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that straight away after having read this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic also asked you yesterday about the forces at Srdj and what you were able to observe. To your knowledge, which forces were stationed at Srdj in December 1991? And I mean by "Srdj," in the area of the Imperijal fortress as opposed to below it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only talk about what I heard. I was not up there, but what I heard was that there were about 30 members of the Territorial Defence up there from Dubrovnik and that they were the ones who bore the brunt of defence against the attack that day, the attack that was carried out with tanks and the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you hear it at the time, that is in December 1991, or at a later point, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I heard that in December, too, as I did later as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yesterday in cross-examination you spoke about your own mobilisation into the Croatian forces after what you described as its recognition by other states. When do you think - and if you don't know just please say so - that the Croatian defence actually became an organised defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your opinion of the date -- when do you say Croatia became recognised internationally? What is your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know; the 15th of January, 1992. Various countries recognised us, and then the Vatican and others, and then it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You also told Mr. Petrovic yesterday that you were living rent free in the building because you take care of it for the owner. Was that the situation in 19 -- in December 1991 as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. Immediately after that, I got this organised from the 7th of December, say from mid-December. There was some construction material that was given to the city by way of aid, and whoever wanted to protect his house from further decay and protect it from rain and snow could do so. So I made an effort and we improvised this temporary roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying by that that you assisted in repairing the roof?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I participated in maintaining the building, and that is the attitude I have until the present day. I treat the building as if it were my own and take good care of it, and therefore the owners respect me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who repaired the damage to the roof of the building, that is Mrs. -- over Mrs. Aleksic's side and over your own side, and when was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main protagonist of this project was the City of Dubrovnik and various humanitarian institutions. As for the form that it takes today, the roof was finally repaired in a thorough fashion sometime about two and a half years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic also asked you about the clothes that Mr. Urban was wearing and the clothes you observed on the body which you say you identified by people saying Pavo Urban has been hit. What's your memory some 12 years and four months later of the clothes he was wearing, or the clothes of the person you saw on the ground was wearing? What's the state of your memory now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had civilian clothes, and it was hard to tell from a 70-metre distance what kind of clothing it was. Usually he wore jeans as trousers. And as for the upper part of his body, usually he wore a shirt and a vest, but that day I could not see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long do you think that you were looking at this body for before you went back inside? That is, how long did you have to record in your mind what the person was wearing, the one who was lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was watching for about ten or 15 seconds when I first went up to the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you first went up to the roof. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first went to the roof about 8.00 in the evening. That's the first time I left this area. It was the first time I went up to the roof. I looked at what had happened on the roof, and then I went out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It may be -- it may be my question wasn't precise enough. I'm asking you about when you looked out the window, to your right onto Stradun, you heard some people saying, "Pavo has been hit," and you saw a body, as you described, lying face down there. How long were you looking at the person for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've already said in response to your -- your previous question, about ten or 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Today Mr. Petrovic cross-examined you about when Mr. Urban was lying there, and you were saying that his colleagues had risked their lives by trying to pull the body away. What was the risk to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He got killed -- I mean, they would have gotten killed because projectiles were falling all over.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P94.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic asked you about the body which you identified yesterday in the photograph of -- as that of Pavo Urban, and you told the Court that he was your friend and you knew him. And your evidence-in-chief yesterday, and in cross-examination, was of seeing him lying, as you said, on his left hip, crouching, facing west. It may seem an obvious question, but does this photograph show the body of the person that you -- in the position that you saw it from your window when you looked right onto the Stradun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not the position that I saw from the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May the exhibit be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again I want to show you a passage and a copy of your statement on which you were cross-examined. This is the statement of the 14th and 18th of September, 2000. I've highlighted a passage in yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to express my concern over the way in which the redirect is taking place. The witness is being given his statement to read out. I think that this is quite wrong in terms of questioning the witness. Could questions please be put to the witness directly in relation to what I cross-examined him about. But for the witness to read out portions of his written statement is quite inappropriate. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It depends on the purpose of the re-examination whether it is proper for the witness to be shown his earlier statement or not, Mr. Petrovic. At the moment it is not clear to me, Mr. Re, what it is you're about to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask him to read, and the reason I've given him the statement rather than my reading it in English and having it translated back to him is to read at that passage in relation to when he saw Mr. Urban's body on the ground and to ask him to -- I'm sorry. Mr. Petrovic put each line of that to the witness. I'm going to ask him to explain each of the lines which were put to him earlier without explanation, without asking for his explanation of them, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that's a proper use of the statement, Mr. Petrovic. That will be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you please look at the highlighted portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And for the record, it's the seventh paragraph on page 3 -- sorry, page 4. That is the third last paragraph on that page and it is the fourth -- sorry, the last paragraph on page 4 of the English there, unnumbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just read that to yourself for a moment. Please read the first line aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "In the course of the day I saw from the window of my apartment when my friend Pavo Urban was hit by a shell, a journalist and photographer."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you mean -- first of all, this is a statement which would -- in which you spoke to an investigator; is that correct? Mr. Arshad.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it was translated. I don't remember. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Trial Chamber what you meant by that line, that is that you saw your friend Pavo Urban was hit by a shell. What do you mean -- what does that line mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question "What do you mean" by something that is in written form is quite inappropriate. The witness was questioned in detail with respect to the circumstances, and he stated his views. So what does the question mean "What do you mean?" "What does that line mean?" It means what it says. I don't see where this examination on the part of Mr. Re is leading to. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wish life was as simple as you put it there, Mr. Petrovic. It is amazing how many times, at least in the English language, words are written and can mean one thing to the writer and another thing to the reader, and I think it is that which Mr. Re is exploring.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my conclusion is based on what it says in the B/C/S version, what this sentence means both logically and grammatically. Thank you for allowing me to make that extra comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re, carry on, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you intend to mean by what is written there? Just that line, the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that I saw Pavo Urban lying underneath the bell tower.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please -- please go to the next sentence which, in English, says: "He was hit when he was at a distance of about 20 metres from my place." Can you just read that out loud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "He was hit some 20 metres from my apartment."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again -- again, what did you intend to mean by what is written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant that from that distance, I was able to see the body lying on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Please go to the next sentence which, in English, says: "He fell down and was lying on his stomach." Please read aloud what it says in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "He fell to the ground on his stomach."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Again, what did you intend to mean by what is recorded in that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was lying face down, stomach down, on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you intend to mean by what is recorded in that statement that you actually saw him being hit by a shell and falling to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I wanted to describe him lying down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wonder, sir, can you tell the Chamber at some time did you actually see the man you've identified or understood to be Pavo Urban lying on the ground near your apartment that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see him standing in that vicinity that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see him falling to the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you saw this person on the ground, will you describe in your words how the body was lying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I described that to Mr. Petrovic already today, so I'll describe it again in the same way, or in a similar way, of course, because you can never describe it the same way. He was lying with his head turned to the south, his legs to the north. He was turned to his left -- on his left hip so that his face -- he was contorted, in a contorted position, and his face was turned towards the west.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was lying on his left side, on his left hip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was lying on his left hip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have difficulty understanding that description and your description that you saw him lying on his stomach. Are you able to explain that further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was in a contorted position so his whole stomach couldn't have been in contact with the ground, but he was lying with a tendency of leaning towards the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, sir, I'm able to tell you now that your evidence is at an end so that you are free now to leave the Chamber and to return to your home. May we thank you for the time and inconvenience that you have suffered to come here, and express our gratitude for your assistance. If you would now go with the court officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you for allowing me to speak in furtherance of what I would call a reconsideration on additional grounds -- excuse me. Correct. It should be private session, if I may. So sorry. I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this a renewal of the application that we heard this morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, and accordingly I would ask if we could return to private session in order to further that application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Are we in private session still?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I ask if we can return for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.43 p.m.,
